name: Peroxycarboxylic (PAP) whitening

lead: PAP (phthalimidoperoxycaproic acid) is a non-peroxide whitening agent sold in some whitening products as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide. People want lighter teeth with less of the sensitivity associated with peroxide.

A peroxycarboxylic acid applied to the teeth oxidises stain compounds, and it can be activated by light or laser. Published human data is one 2025 study of fifteen patients with mild to moderate stains using an 810-nm diode laser.

paras: It is applied to the teeth as a gel or similar product, sometimes with light or laser activation in a clinic setting, and used in place of peroxide whitening. Users typically run it as a short course and compare shade before and after.
Safety and sensitivity data are limited to that small study, and no long-term data were found. As with any whitening product, tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the main things to watch for.

angle.text: PAP is promoted as a peroxide-free way to get lighter teeth with less sensitivity. The agent oxidises stain compounds on the teeth, optionally boosted by light or laser. The published support is one small 2025 laser-activated study of fifteen patients.

lead: PAP whitening uses phthalimidoperoxycaproic acid, a peroxycarboxylic acid marketed as a non-peroxide tooth whitening agent. People use PAP toothpastes, strips, at-home gels and in-office products to lighten tooth shade and remove surface stains for a brighter smile, and it is promoted as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide products, which are associated with tooth sensitivity.[1]

Research is mostly laboratory-based, with one small human study. A 2021 laboratory study of a PAP gel with additives reported that it did not erode enamel or reduce its surface microhardness, unlike hydrogen peroxide and carbamide peroxide gels, and that it performed better than 6% hydrogen peroxide on polyphenol stains in vitro.[2] A 2025 study evaluated PAP activated by an 810-nm diode laser in fifteen patients with mild to moderate stains.[3]
Later 2026 laboratory comparisons on extracted teeth and bovine enamel gave varied results, with PAP matching peroxides in some measures and trailing hydrogen peroxide in others.[4][5][6]
infobox: Whitening toothpastes, strips and gels, including in-office products

paras: Established whitening options are peroxide-based, with sensitivity and gum irritation the commonly reported side effects and peroxide strength regulated differently in the EU and US.[1] PAP products are described as working without generating hydrogen peroxide, which is the basis for their positioning toward sensitive teeth.[2]

A 2025 study in the Journal of Pharmacy & Bioallied Sciences enrolled fifteen patients with shades A2 to A3.5 and mild to moderate stains. After cleaning and polishing, a PAP agent was applied to the front surfaces of upper front teeth and activated with a diode laser. Tooth colour improved significantly immediately and at one month, with minimal adverse effects, but by three months it had reverted to baseline levels, and the authors noted that long-term stability needs further evaluation.[3]
No randomised trial comparing PAP with peroxide whitening in people was found.

A 2021 study in Dentistry Journal tested a PAP+ gel on enamel: it did not erode enamel or reduce surface microhardness compared with hydrogen peroxide and carbamide peroxide gels, and six 10-minute treatments improved shade by about eight VITA Bleachedguide shades on stained enamel.[2]

A 2026 Journal of Dentistry study on 35 human molars compared a PAP gel (combined with papain and bromelain) with 10% carbamide peroxide over 28 days; PAP produced greater whiteness change than untreated controls from day 14, while carbamide peroxide produced higher values from day 7.[4]

A 2026 in vitro study on extracted incisors found lightness increases of 7.19 units for hydrogen peroxide, 7.11 for PAP and 4.43 for carbamide peroxide, with PAP showing less enamel microhardness reduction.[5] A 2026 study on stained bovine blocks found PAP, with or without LED light, did not differ from untreated controls, while 10% hydrogen peroxide bleached more.[6] A 2024 study found peroxide-free in-office bleaching left the surface properties of CAD/CAM restorative materials unchanged, while peroxide-based bleaching roughened some.[7]
